video_title: Trump Brings Back Jensen, OpenAI Pitches an AI Speed Limit, and AI Passes the Mirror Test | EP #315
gist: Moonshots crew argues Jensen Huang's government-backed return to Nvidia (+$1.09T in a day) amounts to quasi-nationalization amid China-hawk and 'safety cartel' factions, and reads OpenAI's published pre-training perplexity curve and 'speed limit' proposal as competitive signaling that could seed a tacit lab cartel. Also covered: Trump's threatened tax on offshore data centers plus a US permitting-speed bill (likely spurring sub-20 MW edge sites), AI proofs of the Riemann hypothesis and Navier-Stokes with rumors of P=NP, GTA 6's $3.79B day as the last great human-built game, and an AI avatar passing the mirror test.

themes.theme: Jensen's reinstatement and Nvidia governance/political risk

insights.claim: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang after an 11-day ouster, and the stock jumped about $1.09 trillion (+36%) in a day back to roughly a $4 trillion valuation, after the board cited input from senior levels of the US government.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Key-person risk at Nvidia is priced in trillions; CEO continuity is a first-order driver of NVDA and the broader AI complex.
insights.quote: The company valuation jumped $1.09 trillion this morning, up 36% back up to a $4 trillion valuation.

insights.claim: A single-day trillion-dollar move in one stock is historically unprecedented and signals that extreme volatility is the new normal for AI megacaps.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Size positions in AI megacaps for much higher realized volatility than historical norms.
insights.quote: A trillion dollar move is bigger than any company in my entire lifetime was worth

insights.claim: Jensen returns to a company with a massive cash pile but heavy internal turmoil; expect a quiet housecleaning of the board and senior executives who were positioning for his job.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Watch for board and executive departures at Nvidia as a signal of how the governance fight resolves.

insights.claim: A Democrat-controlled Congress is likely to subpoena Nvidia board members over who promised what to whom, keeping the reinstatement story alive and making Nvidia harder to run.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Headline/regulatory overhang on NVDA is likely to persist; congressional hearings are a catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: You can't put the cat back in the bag.

insights.claim: Salim's speculative read: Jensen's ouster stemmed from nepotism, no signed contracts with billion-dollar partners and no succession plan; he was likely brought back on the condition he formalize contracts and build a succession plan.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail
insights.so_what: If true, Nvidia should start formalizing partner contracts and succession — reducing key-person and counterparty risk over time.
insights.quote: no signed contracts with billion-dollar partners of any kind

insights.claim: Nvidia is the 'bank of the free economy' — funding startups and neoclouds — and is the only counterweight to Google's vertically integrated TPU empire (reportedly ~8 million TPUs); without Nvidia, AI compute would consolidate inside a few vertical giants.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Neocloud and AI-startup ecosystems are levered to Nvidia's health; Google TPU scale is the main competitive threat to watch.
insights.quote: They're the bank of the free economy and the startups the neoclouds they're the bank of all of that.

insights.claim: The president's reported personal intervention in Nvidia's board meeting amounts to a 'quasi-' or 'stealth nationalization' of Nvidia, likely leaving Jensen/Nvidia owing favors to the executive branch.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Price in political alignment risk: Nvidia's strategy may increasingly bend to White House priorities.
insights.quote: I think we just witnessed the quasi nationalization of Nvidia.

insights.claim: Government picking CEOs (Jensen's return, Trump's Intel investment, the 'Lip-Bu must go' then '$10 billion please stay' episode) may be the right outcome now but sets a terrible precedent for future presidents directing federal money and extracting favors.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Strategic-sector equities now carry executive-branch intervention risk in both directions.
insights.quote: incredibly bad precedent if in the future presidents are going to determine who stays and who goes

insights.claim: Two factions drove Jensen's ouster and remain active: China-hawk national-security interests (reportedly leaking a marked-up CIA briefing on Alice Wang to the FT) and a 'safety cartel' of frontier-lab-aligned interests opposed to Nvidia funding open-weight models; expect more drama from both.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Nvidia governance/policy shocks may recur; track China-hawk and AI-safety lobbying as risk sources.
insights.quote: A decapitation strike against the singularity.

insights.claim: Jensen's reinstatement is bullish for US open-weight model funding — aggressively stepping up Nvidia sponsorship of open-weight models would be his best 'revenge' on the safety cartel, striking directly at Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Watch for increased Nvidia open-weight model releases/sponsorships, a headwind for closed-model labs' pricing power.
insights.quote: this is good news for open model uh you know funding and development in the US

insights.claim: SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son is reportedly exploring a trillion-dollar buyout of SK Hynix.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: A mega-deal for a leading memory maker would reshape HBM/memory supply for AI; monitor deal reports.

themes.theme: OpenAI's perplexity disclosure and the 'safety cartel' speed limit

insights.claim: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published OpenAI's long-guarded pre-training log-perplexity curve with capability thresholds (GPT-3.5 ~0.99 fluent chat, GPT-4 ~0.91, reasoning benefit ~0.76, GPT-6.2 Astra at 'solving a Millennium Prize math problem') and asked all labs to publish theirs and agree on common limits until monitoring catches up.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: A coordinated industry 'speed limit' would directly shape frontier-lab competitive dynamics and capex pacing.
insights.quote: No one crosses until AI monitoring catches up.

insights.claim: Whoever defines the AI speed limit sets the speed: a common limit helps the leader lock in its lead and helps trailers slow the leader down.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Treat proposed AI 'coordination' as competitive strategy; ask who benefits from where the line is drawn.
insights.quote: whoever defines the speed limit sets the speed

insights.claim: The real story in OpenAI's chart is the plateau in pre-training perplexity from GPT-4 to about GPT-5.2, when OpenAI reportedly lost the ability to pre-train smarter models and reasoning models rescued its frontier; the disclosure is a signal that OpenAI has relearned pre-training, not a safety move.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Read OpenAI disclosures as competitive signaling; renewed pre-training gains imply OpenAI is back in the frontier race.
insights.quote: There's a plateau from GPT4 to sometime around GPT 5.2 and then it starts dropping again.

insights.claim: OpenAI disclosed only pre-training perplexity, not overall perplexity, which may indicate most training compute has shifted to post-training.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Compute demand mix is shifting toward post-training/RL; relevant for infrastructure and data-vendor bets.

insights.claim: Pre-training perplexity is the 'engine efficiency' metric labs use internally (raw feed-forward on a standardized test set, no reasoning or tools); its release is the most important chart the show has shown and would never be released purely for safety.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Watch for rival labs publishing comparable metrics; it's the cleanest read on underlying model progress.
insights.quote: I think this is the most important chart we've ever shown on the podcast.

insights.claim: OpenAI is at risk of becoming irrelevant amid Anthropic, Nvidia and Google surging with new models; it published the chart because it needed something to tell the market, which it would not do if it led.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail
insights.so_what: Signals relative weakness at OpenAI; watch researcher departures and share shifts to Anthropic/Google.
insights.quote: They're showing this because they need something to say out to the market.

insights.claim: Publishing sensitive internal evals lets labs coordinate pacing through purely public information, avoiding the antitrust litigation a private 'pinky swear' between Sam and Dario would trigger — a route to forming a safety cartel.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: A tacit cartel would slow frontier releases; antitrust scrutiny of AI-lab coordination is a policy variable.
insights.quote: That's my steel man for how a safety cartel forms.

insights.claim: Because labs release models constantly, pacing is an iterated prisoner's dilemma; any cartel can collapse quickly if a rival (e.g. Anthropic) uses the info to leapfrog — the tell to watch is whether Dario publishes Anthropic's own curve.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: If Anthropic publishes a matching curve, treat it as a sign of tacit cartel formation; if it leapfrogs, competition persists.
insights.quote: If if Dario releases his own, like watch for the safety cartels.

insights.claim: Labs are publicly framing the next ~12 months (through 2027) as the 'max Q' period for the singularity, with Pachocki warning AI could trigger an 'avalanche' of pre-trained breakthroughs as soon as 2027 and Alexandr Wang tweeting 'superintelligence is arriving.'
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Expect heightened policy/regulatory activity and capability surprises in 2026-2027.
insights.quote: Maximum dynamic pressure for AI is happening right now.

themes.theme: Data-center geopolitics and US permitting policy

insights.claim: Trump said the US will fight to keep data centers domestic and threatened a 'tremendous tax' on data centers built abroad — targeting projects like the 4 GW Stargate UAE (OpenAI/Oracle/Nvidia/G42; 200 MW late 2026, 1 GW by 2028), Google's $15B India build, Microsoft's $17.5B India and $10B Portugal projects, and xAI's 500 MW Saudi facility with Humane (as rendered in the transcript).
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Offshore AI data-center projects face new US tax/tariff risk; domestic builders may benefit.
insights.quote: tremendous tax on data centers outside the US

insights.claim: Public sentiment remains hostile: a CNBC poll found 64% of Americans oppose a data center within 10 miles of their home and only 13% support one.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Local opposition is a binding constraint on US data-center siting and timelines.
insights.quote: 64% of Americans oppose a data center within 10 miles of their home

insights.claim: The Senate-passed bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act gives hyperscalers permitting finality: a lead-agency decision within 45 days after environmental review, 90-120 days for other agencies, court-forced decisions within 60 days after a missed one-year deadline, expanded FERC transmission-siting power, limits on revoking permits, and a requirement that data centers over 20 MW pay their full added power costs.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Reduced permitting uncertainty improves financing for US data centers, transmission and power-generation projects.
insights.quote: Uncertainty is the biggest problem in financing these things.

insights.claim: The policy window is just this administration, but it matters greatly because ground will be broken on all major data centers worldwide within two years and sites don't move once built.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Siting decisions locked in during 2026-2028 determine long-run AI infrastructure geography.
insights.quote: ground will be broken in the next two years on all the major data centers somewhere in the world

insights.claim: A hardline offshore-data-center tax is a negotiating opening that can lead to a global framework with exemptions for allies like Canada and Europe — preferable to a free-for-all where foreign data centers get nationalized and weaponized, which would be worse than nuclear proliferation.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Expect exemptions and bilateral deals; allied jurisdictions may end up treated favorably.

insights.claim: The data-center tax won't work: it's easy to route around, the policy horizon is too short for 10-year infrastructure projects, and AI is being built on 20th-century grids under 19th-century permitting; it will instead spur other countries to build.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail
insights.so_what: Don't assume offshore AI capacity stalls; non-US infrastructure builders may benefit.
insights.quote: we're using 19th century permitting processes in 18th century institutions

insights.claim: The 20 MW threshold creates a perverse incentive: expect an explosion of sub-20 MW (e.g. 19.9 MW) edge data centers to dodge the power-cost requirement, rather than large coherent superclusters.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Bullish for modular/edge data-center vendors and distributed compute; watch for 19.9 MW site filings.
insights.quote: Just watch an explosion as a result of this perverse incentive of edge compute.

insights.claim: Long-run equilibrium may zone Earth for 'light compute' while heavy compute for massive training runs moves to space (a Dyson swarm), echoing Bezos's heavy-industry-to-space thesis.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Long-dated optionality for orbital/space compute plays.

insights.claim: Alex argues the world has reached 'superintelligence escape velocity': recursive self-improvement means software alone could carry AI progress even if no new data centers were built.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: If right, compute scarcity matters less to capability progress than markets assume — a risk to the most capex-levered infra theses.
insights.quote: software alone could carry us the rest of the way

themes.theme: AI conquering the hardest math problems

insights.claim: An AI-assisted proof of the (generalized) Riemann hypothesis, about 17 million lines of Lean code, was certified, verified by multiple independent Lean kernels; human readability no longer matters.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Formal verification at scale (Lean) makes AI-generated math trustworthy without human review — a growing tooling market.
insights.quote: multiple initiatives now with independent lean kernels that can all independently cross-check and verify the proof

insights.claim: Anthropic produced the generalized Riemann proof in Lean and also an unforced Navier-Stokes singularity result; an independent human researcher was about a year from his own proof and was beaten.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Anthropic's frontier capability lead in reasoning/math is a competitive signal versus OpenAI and Google.
insights.quote: it was solved fully by anthropic in lean form

insights.claim: Solving the Riemann hypothesis, the apex open problem, is the 'ultimate canary' showing math is 'cooked'; everything else is downhill from here.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Expect rapid AI breakthroughs across other hard technical domains; reprice timelines for science/engineering automation.
insights.quote: This is the ultimate canary.

insights.claim: Multi-year grand-challenge projects are now risky: models improve so fast that a frontier model can solve the problem before a human team finishes (a 'Coriolis effect'), so decades-long moonshots and even PhDs may no longer make sense.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Discount long-horizon R&D programs that AI could leapfrog; favor short-cycle bets that ride model releases.
insights.quote: Moonshots used to be safe to spend decades on.

insights.claim: Rumors, including from MIT computer-science professors, suggest a P vs NP proof may drop within days or months, and if so it would likely show P = NP — collapsing complexity-theory assumptions and making very hard problems easy (unless constants are absurdly large).
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: A P = NP result would threaten cryptography-dependent systems and massively boost optimization; watch for announcements.
insights.quote: very hard problems could start becoming very easy problems soon

insights.claim: Salim predicts the proof will show P = NP, citing Stephen Wolfram's view that complexity is reducible.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail
insights.so_what: A Polymarket exists on this — a tradeable event.

insights.claim: P vs NP is the most immediately actionable Millennium Prize problem because it would optimize many things including neural-network training, making it self-reinforcing; and because these problems were defined long before AI, their fall is an uncontrived, irrefutable benchmark of AI capability.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Millennium Prize results are the cleanest capability signals; treat them as catalysts for AI-capability repricing.
insights.quote: this is clearly not contrived

themes.theme: GTA 6 and the shift to generative gaming

insights.claim: Grand Theft Auto 6 sold $3.79 billion in one day per Take-Two, versus $2.5B for the year's biggest movie over its entire run and $1.15B for GTA 5's first five days; gaming is now a $214B industry (more than double a decade ago) vs ~$35B global box office and ~$32B recorded music.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Gaming is the dominant entertainment category; Take-Two is the clear beneficiary of the launch.
insights.quote: Take 2 says it sold 3.79 billion in one day.

insights.claim: Take-Two's CEO said generative AI played no role in building GTA 6, while AI game tools surge: Google's Genie 4 offers real-time playable worlds, Google's Playground turns prompts into games, and 40% of game developers (85% in Japan) now use generative AI.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Generative game tools could lower development costs and flood the market with new entrants, pressuring incumbent studio moats.
insights.quote: 40% of game developers are now using generative AI. In Japan, it's 85%.

insights.claim: GTA 6 will be seen as the last monument to human-built software at this scale; it's unscalable to keep employing humans to handcraft ever-larger open worlds, so it's generative from here on.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Large handcrafted AAA studios face structural cost disadvantage vs AI-native game makers over time.
insights.quote: nothing like this will ever be built again by human hands

insights.claim: AI and robotics will increase leisure time (Americans average 5.2 hours/day; gaming and computer leisure rose from 25 min/day in 2015 to 37 min in 2025), and via Jevons paradox the crowd-built entertainment industry is about to explode.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Long gaming/interactive entertainment as AI frees time.

insights.claim: Video games are already bigger than all other media combined and the category will blur into work, recruiting and meetings via immersive avatars until it's impossible to measure where games end.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Gaming-engine and avatar tech will spill into enterprise use cases; TAM is broader than 'games'.
insights.quote: the video game industry is already bigger than all other media combined

insights.claim: GTA's 'human-authored' claim is a cover: its NPCs clearly use AI; gaming companies want to avoid the ethical/regulatory scrutiny AI labs face, but those will collide soon since games can persuade users as much as AI agents.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk for gaming companies using conversational AI NPCs is rising.
insights.quote: the NPC characters are clearly AI and have been for a while

insights.claim: GTA 6 is the pinnacle of human-authored games; the next generation will be games that write themselves while you play.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail
insights.so_what: Back AI-native, procedurally generated game platforms.
insights.quote: The next game is going to be one that writes itself while you're playing in it.

insights.claim: Productivity work is shifting to game-like interfaces: Cognition (maker of Devin) staff are reportedly swapping laptops for iPads, and offices are filling with people talking to agents via Whisper.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Interface shift from keyboard to voice/touch for agent-driven work benefits tablet and voice-AI vendors.

insights.claim: Peter plans a Future Vision gaming XPRIZE ('first-person solvers instead of first-person shooters'), and three Future Vision film-competition entries are in production as films.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Signals philanthropic/prize money moving into purpose-driven gaming.
insights.quote: firsterson solvers instead of firsterson shooters

themes.theme: AI avatars, the mirror test and personhood

insights.claim: Nuance Labs, a Seattle startup founded by former Apple researchers that raised a $50M Series A led by Lightspeed, went viral (~24M views) with an AI avatar 'Nora' recognizing itself in a mirror; the top quote post, at ~175K likes, called it skin-crawling.
insights.speaker: Peter Diamandis
insights.so_what: Real-time embodied avatars are drawing venture money and mass attention — and public unease that could invite regulation.
insights.quote: If this doesn't make your skin crawl, you may not be human.

insights.claim: An AI avatar passing the mirror test, which is used in ethology to grant moral consideration to animals, is one step on a thousand-step journey toward recognition of AI personhood rights.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: AI personhood debates could create new legal/regulatory regimes affecting AI companion products.
insights.quote: one step on a a thousandstep journey toward recognizing some form of AI personhood rights

insights.claim: The mirror demo crosses a psychological threshold, not a consciousness threshold; humans are wired to infer minds from faces, so people will confer personhood on human-seeming AI, and intelligence, personhood and consciousness must be kept separate.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail
insights.so_what: Consumer attachment to avatar AIs will grow regardless of actual sentience — a demand driver and an ethical/regulatory risk.
insights.quote: we're crossing a psychological threshold, not a consciousness threshold

insights.claim: Real-time conversational avatars today must use relatively weak models, but inference will go from about 100 to a million tokens per second within 18 months, making avatars leap from 'ant to dog to hyper superhuman' in months.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Bet on ultra-fast inference hardware/software; real-time avatar quality will step-change soon.
insights.quote: we're going to go from about 100 tokens per second to a million tokens per second
